k1-intro.text: French has two verbs you need from the very first day: *être* (to be) and *avoir* (to have). With them you say who you are, where you are from, how old you are and what you have.

k1-why.text: They are the most common French verbs, and they also build the past tense (Chapter 8): *j'ai mangé, je suis venu*. Some things that are “be” in English take *avoir* in French: *J'ai 30 ans. J'ai faim.*
k1-why.title: Why is this so important?

k1-h1.text: Subject pronouns and the two verbs

k1-rule1.text: A French verb always needs a subject: a noun or a pronoun. You can't leave it out: *Je suis fatigué*, never *Suis fatigué*. *Je* becomes *j'* before a vowel or a silent h: *j'ai, j'habite*.

k1-m1.text: *Tu* is for friends, family, children and colleagues who say *tu* to you. *Vous* is for one person you don't know well, and for any group: at the préfecture, at the doctor's or with a landlord, always start with *vous*. *On* takes the *il* form and in speech often means “we”: *On est en retard.* *Ils* is for men or a mixed group, *elles* only for women.

k1-h2.text: être: who, what, where and how

head: Use
Example
cells: what someone or something is like

k1-h3.text: avoir: what you have, and more

k1-m2.text: A plain job needs no article after *être*: *Je suis infirmière.* After *c'est*, use one: *C'est une très bonne infirmière.* Your age always goes with *avoir* and *ans*: *J'ai 25 ans.*

k1-err.text: In French your age goes with *avoir*, never with *être*.

k2-intro.text: We use the présent for habits and facts, for what is happening now (French has no separate “-ing” form), and often for the near future: *J'habite à Lyon. Karim travaille la nuit. Demain, je travaille l'après-midi.*

k2-rule1.text: Most French verbs end in *-er* in the dictionary: *parler, travailler, habiter*. Take off *-er* and add the ending for the person.

k2-m1.text: Four forms sound exactly the same: *parle, parles, parle, parlent* (the *-s* and *-ent* are silent). You only hear *nous parlons* and *vous parlez* as different. Before a vowel, the *s* of *nous, vous, ils, elles* is said as a z: *ils aiment* sounds like “il-zem”.

k2-rule2.text: Verbs in *-ger* keep an *e* before *-ons*: *nous mangeons*. Verbs in *-cer* take a *ç*: *nous commençons*. A few verbs change their stem with *je, tu, il* and *ils*: *acheter → j'achète*, *appeler → j'appelle*, *payer → je paie*.

k2-h4.text: How often? Words that often go with the présent

k2-m2.text: *Le lundi* means every Monday: *Le lundi, je travaille à la maison.* *Lundi* with no article means this coming Monday: *Lundi, j'ai rendez-vous.* French uses no word for “on” here.

k2-err.text: The form in *-er* is only the dictionary form. In a sentence, the verb takes the ending for the person.

k3-intro.text: French has three ways to ask a question, from relaxed to formal, and a negative in two parts: *ne … pas*. French needs no helping verb like “do” for either.

k3-why.text: Asking is how you get things done: at the mairie, at the doctor's, at the bank. With a few question words and *ne … pas*, you can ask for what you need and say what is not the case.
k3-why.title: Why is this so important?

k3-rule1.text: Say a normal sentence and let your voice rise, or put *est-ce que* in front (*est-ce qu'* before a vowel). Swapping the verb and the pronoun, with a hyphen, is formal. All three mean the same.

k3-rule2.text: In everyday speech the question word often goes at the end: *Tu habites où ?* With *est-ce que* it goes first: *Où est-ce que tu habites ?* The formal way swaps verb and pronoun: *Où habitez-vous ?* A preposition stays with the question word: *Tu es d'où ? Tu habites avec qui ?*
k3-rule2.title: The question word: at the end or at the start

head: Question word
Asks about
Example
cells: the way, what it is like
a price, an amount, a number

k3-m1.text: *Pourquoi ?* asks why; *parce que* answers: *Pourquoi tu apprends le français ? Parce que j'habite ici.* *Quel* agrees with its noun, and all four forms sound the same: *Quel âge avez-vous ? Quelle est votre date de naissance ?*

k3-rule3.text: Put *ne* before the verb and *pas* after it: *Je ne travaille pas.* *Ne* becomes *n'* before a vowel: *Je n'habite pas ici.* A short answer: *Tu travailles aujourd'hui ? Non, je ne travaille pas.*

k3-rule4.text: Replace *pas* with another word to say more. After a negative, *un, une, des* and *du, de la* become *de* (*d'* before a vowel): *J'ai une voiture* but *Je n'ai pas de voiture.*

k3-m2.text: In everyday speech people often drop *ne*: *Je sais pas. C'est pas grave.* You will hear it all the time, but in writing, in an exam or at the préfecture, use both parts. In informal Québec French you may also hear *-tu* in questions: *Tu viens-tu ?*

k3-err.text: After a negative, *un, une, des* become *de*. With *être* they stay: *Ce n'est pas une voiture, c'est un vélo.*

k4-intro.text: Every French noun is masculine or feminine, also words for things. Articles and adjectives change to match the noun: *le petit appartement, la petite maison, les petits appartements, les petites maisons*.

k4-rule1.text: The ending of a noun often helps, but there are many exceptions. The safest way: learn every noun with *un* or *une*. (*Le* and *la* both become *l'* before a vowel, so *l'* doesn't show the gender.)

k4-m1.text: Common traps: *le problème, le musée, le lycée* are masculine; *la page, la plage, l'image, la fin* are feminine. Job names often have two forms: *un infirmier, une infirmière; un vendeur, une vendeuse*.

k4-rule2.text: French almost always puts an article before a noun, also for things in general where English has none: *J'aime le café. Les enfants jouent beaucoup.* For an amount of something you don't count, use *du, de la, de l'*: *Je bois du café. Tu veux de l'eau ?* A plain job after *être* takes no article: *Elle est médecin.*

k4-m2.text: *à* + *le* = *au*, *à* + *les* = *aux*, *de* + *le* = *du*, *de* + *les* = *des*: *Je vais au travail. Je parle aux enfants. Je viens du marché.* Not with *la* or *l'*: *Je vais à la pharmacie, à l'hôpital.*

k4-rule3.text: Most adjectives go after the noun and agree with it: add *-e* for feminine and *-s* for plural. A few short, common ones go before the noun: *grand, petit, bon, beau, nouveau, jeune, vieux*. For a mixed group of men and women, use the masculine plural.

k4-h5.text: il y a, or est / sont?

k4-rule4.text: *Il y a* means “there is” and “there are”, and it never changes. Use it for new information, with *un, une, des*, a number or *du, de la*. For a particular thing you already know, use *est* or *sont*.

k4-err.text: *Voiture* is feminine, so the article and the adjective are feminine too. The noun itself doesn't always show it: learn it with *un* or *une*.

k5-intro.text: The most common French verbs are irregular. Learn them early: you need them in almost every sentence, and many of them follow one of a few patterns.

k5-m1.text: *Aller* goes with *à* for a place and *chez* for a person: *Je vais à Paris. Je vais chez le médecin.* *Faire* is in many fixed phrases: *faire les courses, faire la cuisine, Il fait froid.* *Prendre* is for transport and for food and drink: *Je prends le bus. Je prends un café.*

k5-rule1.text: Regular *-ir* verbs add *-iss-* in the plural: *je finis, nous finissons, ils finissent*. A second group drops the last consonant of the stem in the singular: *partir → je pars, nous partons*. *Sortir* and *dormir* work the same way.

k5-rule2.text: In many irregular verbs the three singular forms sound the same (*je dis, tu dis, il dit*), and the plural has a longer stem (*nous disons, ils disent*). Learn the *je*, *nous* and *ils* forms together.

k5-m2.text: *Savoir* is to know a fact or how to do something: *Je sais conduire. Je ne sais pas.* *Connaître* is to know a person or a place: *Je connais Lyon. Je connais bien ta sœur.*

k5-err.text: *Faire* has an irregular *vous* form: *vous faites*. So do *dire* (*vous dites*) and *être* (*vous êtes*).

k6-intro.text: French has small pronouns (*me, te, se, le, la, lui…*) that go right before the verb. This chapter shows the two patterns you use every day: reflexive verbs and object pronouns.

k6-rule2.text: These verbs have *se* in front in the dictionary: *se lever, s'appeler*. The pronoun changes with the person and goes before the verb. Many of them describe your daily routine. *Me, te, se* become *m', t', s'* before a vowel or a silent h.

k6-m2.text: In the negative, *ne* comes before the pronoun: *Je ne me lève pas tôt.* With an infinitive, the pronoun still matches the person: *Je vais me coucher. Tu dois te reposer.*

k6-rule3.text: An object pronoun replaces a person or a thing, so you don't repeat it. A direct object answers “what?” or “who?”: *Je vois Léa* becomes *Je la vois.* An indirect object is a person after *à*: *Je parle à Léa* becomes *Je lui parle.* Only the third person has different forms.

k6-m3.text: The pronoun goes before the verb, also in the negative: *Je ne le vois pas.* With two verbs, it goes before the infinitive: *Je vais l'appeler.* In the past tense it goes before *avoir* or *être*: *Je l'ai vu.*

k6-m4.text: Watch the verb, not the English. *Attendre, chercher, écouter, regarder* take a direct object: *J'attends le bus. Je l'attends.* *Téléphoner à, parler à, répondre à, demander à* take an indirect one: *Je téléphone à ma mère. Je lui téléphone.*

k6-err.text: In French the object pronoun goes before the verb, not after it as in English.

k7-intro.text: Many everyday meanings come from two verbs together. Only the first verb changes; the second stays in the infinitive.

head: Verb
Meaning
Example
cells: have to, must: you or someone in particular
you have to: a rule for everybody
can: a skill you have learned

k7-rule1.text: The first verb takes the ending for the person; the infinitive never changes. *Il faut* has only this one form. *Ne … pas* goes around the first verb: *Je ne peux pas venir.*

k7-m1.text: *Tu ne dois pas fumer ici* and *Il ne faut pas fumer ici* = you must not. For “you don't have to”, say *Tu n'es pas obligé de venir*. *Je sais conduire* = I know how; *Aujourd'hui, je ne peux pas conduire* = today I can't. To ask politely, use *je voudrais*: *Je voudrais un rendez-vous.*

k7-rule2.text: This is the most common way to talk about plans. Use the présent of *aller* (Chapter 5), then the infinitive.

k7-h3.text: être en train de: what is happening right now

k7-rule3.text: French has no “-ing” form for now: the plain présent says it. *Je mange* = I eat or I am eating. To stress that something is going on at this very moment, use *être en train de* + infinitive.

k7-m2.text: *Venir de* + infinitive says that something has just happened: *Je viens d'arriver* = I have just arrived. It is the opposite of *aller* + infinitive.

k7-err.text: After *il faut, devoir, pouvoir, vouloir* and *aller*, the second verb stays in the infinitive.

k8-intro.text: The *passé composé* is the everyday past tense: it says what happened. English has two tenses here (*I ate* and *I have eaten*); French uses the *passé composé* for both: *J'ai mangé.*

k8-rule1.text: Most verbs use the présent of *avoir* and the past participle. *-er* verbs take *-é*: *parler → parlé*. Regular *-ir* verbs take *-i*: *finir → fini*. In the negative, *ne … pas* goes around *avoir*: *Je n'ai pas mangé.*

k8-rule2.text: About twenty verbs take *être* instead of *avoir*: mostly verbs of moving or of a change of state, and all reflexive verbs. With *être*, the participle agrees with the subject like an adjective: *Il est arrivé. Elle est arrivée. Ils sont arrivés.*

k8-m1.text: *Vous* for one woman: *Vous êtes allée.* For a mixed group, use the masculine plural: *Mes parents sont partis.* With *avoir*, the participle usually doesn't change: *Elle a mangé.* (The exception, with a pronoun before *avoir*, comes at B2.)

k8-rule3.text: The *passé composé* goes with words for finished time and for experience: *hier, ce matin, la semaine dernière, en 2019, il y a deux jours, déjà, jamais*. *Il y a* + a time means “ago”: *Je suis arrivé en France il y a trois ans.*

head: Rule
Example
cells: short adverbs go between avoir / être and the participle
ne … pas goes around avoir / être
time words at the start or at the end

k8-err.text: With *être*, the participle agrees with the subject: add *-e* for a woman and *-s* for more than one.

k9-intro.text: The *imparfait* describes the past: what things were like, what was going on, what used to happen. Together with the *passé composé*, which says what happened next, it lets you tell a story.

k9-rule1.text: Take the *nous* form of the présent, drop *-ons* and add *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*: *nous parlons → je parlais*, *nous finissons → je finissais*, *nous faisons → je faisais*. Only *être* is irregular: *j'étais*.

k9-m3.text: Four endings sound the same: *parlais, parlais, parlait, parlaient*. Verbs in *-ger* and *-cer* keep their sound before *a*: *je mangeais, je commençais* (but *nous mangions, nous commencions*).

head: Use
Example
cells: a habit, what used to happen
age, time and weather in the past
an action that was going on

k9-m1.text: *Avant* + *imparfait* is the usual way to say “used to”: *Avant, j'habitais en Roumanie ; maintenant, j'habite à Strasbourg.*

k9-rule2.text: Think of a film. The *imparfait* is the background: the scene and the situation. The *passé composé* gives the events that move the story on.

k9-m2.text: A finished period with a clear length takes the *passé composé*: *J'ai habité dix ans à Rabat* (and then I left). Compare: *J'habitais à Rabat quand j'ai rencontré mon mari.*

k9-err.text: The time in the past is background, so it takes the *imparfait*.

k10-intro.text: This chapter brings together four things you need at B1: the *futur simple*, the *conditionnel*, sentences with *si*, and your first steps with the *subjonctif*. Each section shows the basic form; there is more practice online.

k10-rule1.text: Add *-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont* to the infinitive; *-re* verbs drop their final *e*: *prendre → je prendrai*. Use it for predictions, promises and plans further away. For near plans, people usually say *aller* + infinitive (Chapter 7).

k10-m3.text: After *quand* with a future meaning, French uses the *futur*, not the present as English does: *Quand j'aurai mes papiers, je chercherai un appartement.*

k10-rule2.text: It has the same stem as the *futur*, with the endings of the *imparfait*: *-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient*. So: *je parlerais, j'aurais, je voudrais, je pourrais*. Use it to sound polite and to imagine something.

k10-rule3.text: *Si* + présent, then a présent, a *futur* or an imperative. Use this for things that can really happen. *Si* becomes *s'* before *il* and *ils*, not before *elle*: *S'il pleut… Si elle vient…*

k10-m1.text: There is never a *futur* or a *conditionnel* right after *si* when it means “if”: *Si j'ai le temps, je t'appellerai*, not *Si j'aurai le temps*. Imagined conditions (*Si j'avais…, je ferais…*) come at B2.

k10-rule4.text: Start from the *ils* form of the présent, drop *-ent* and add *-e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent*: *ils parlent → que je parle*, *ils finissent → que je finisse*, *ils viennent → que je vienne*. The *nous* and *vous* forms look like the *imparfait*: *que nous venions*.

head: When
Example
cells: a wish for someone else: je veux que, je voudrais que
a feeling: je suis content que, j'ai peur que

k10-m2.text: Same person: infinitive. *Je veux partir.* Different person: *que* + subjonctif. *Je veux que tu partes.* After *je pense que, je crois que* and *j'espère que*, use the normal indicative: *Je pense qu'il vient. J'espère que tu vas bien.*

k10-err.text: After *il faut que*, the verb is in the *subjonctif*.
